extracted.intended_audience: graduate students or advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions and basic properties around Spec A, irreducible/connected components, Noetherian conditions, the V/I correspondences, the structure sheaf OSpec A, and the definition of schemes (affine and general). Includes exercises and illustrative examples for intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreducible component
rubrics_metrics.description: An irreducible component of a topological space is a maximal irreducible subset (an irreducible subset not contained in any larger irreducible subset). Irreducible components are closed (as the closure of irreducible subsets are irreducible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of irreducible components of X as maximal among irreducible closed subsets; they are the 'pieces of X'. (Figure 3.9.) Exercises: closure of an irreducible subset is irreducible (Exercise 3.6.B(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Connected component
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset Y of a topological space X is a connected component if it is a maximal connected subset (a connected subset not contained in any larger connected subset).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every point is contained in a connected component; connected components are always closed. However, connected components need not be open in general (Remark 3.6.13); in Noetherian spaces connected components are open (Exercise 3.6.Q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of irreducible components through every point
rubrics_metrics.description: Every point x of a topological space X is contained in an irreducible component of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Zorn's Lemma: consider the partially ordered set of irreducible closed subsets containing x and choose a maximal totally ordered subset {Z_alpha}; show the union is irreducible (Exercise 3.6.O).

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian topological space
rubrics_metrics.description: A topological space X is called Noetherian if it satisfies the descending chain condition for closed subsets: any sequence Z1 ⊃ Z2 ⊃ ··· of closed subsets eventually stabilizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences/exercises: In many examples (e.g. spectra of Noetherian rings) spaces break into finitely many irreducible components. Example: C^2 with the classical topology is not Noetherian (Exercise 3.6.P). Every open subset of a Noetherian topological space is quasicompact (Exercise 3.6.T).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique finite decomposition into irreducibles (Noetherian spaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a Noetherian topological space, then every nonempty closed subset Z can be expressed uniquely as a finite union Z = Z1 ∪ ··· ∪ Zr of irreducible closed subsets, none contained in any other (Proposition 3.6.15).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Noetherian induction: consider closed subsets that cannot be expressed as a finite union, choose a minimal counterexample, and derive contradiction by writing it as union of two proper closed subsets. Uniqueness argument: compare two representations and show they refine each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian ring (definition and equivalent finite-generation property)
rubrics_metrics.description: A ring is Noetherian if every ascending sequence of ideals eventually stabilizes (ascending chain condition on ideals). Equivalent condition: every ideal of A is finitely generated (Exercise 3.6.R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick facts: fields and Z are Noetherian; Noetherianness is preserved by quotients and localizations. If A is Noetherian then Spec A is a Noetherian topological space (Exercise 3.6.S).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert Basis Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is Noetherian, then so is A[x] (Theorem 3.6.17).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vakil's proof: produce generators of an ideal in A[x] inductively by degree; use Noetherianness of A on leading coefficients to force termination. Consequence: polynomial rings over fields or Z and their quotients/localizations are Noetherian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and non-examples of Noetherian rings
rubrics_metrics.description: Most 'nice' rings are Noetherian, e.g. polynomial rings in finitely many variables over a field or Z; but some rings are not Noetherian, e.g. k[x1,x2,...] (infinite polynomial ring) because (x1) ⊂ (x1,x2) ⊂ (x1,x2,x3) ⊂ ···.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also note: Spec A may be Noetherian even if A is not (example given via quotient making Spec one point) (Exercise 3.6.S).

rubrics_metrics.name: V and I correspondence between closed sets and radical ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: V(·) and I(·) give an inclusion-reversing bijection between closed subsets of Spec A and radical ideals of A: a closed subset S maps to the radical ideal I(S), and a radical ideal J maps to the closed subset V(J) (Theorem 3.7.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts: I(S) is always a radical ideal; V(I(S)) = S for closed S; I(V(J)) = √J (Exercise 3.7.D). These show V and I are 'almost' inverses on closed sets/radical ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence between irreducible closed subsets and prime ideals (generic points)
rubrics_metrics.description: V(·) and I(·) give a bijection between irreducible closed subsets of Spec A and prime ideals of A. Consequently there is a bijection between points of Spec A and irreducible closed subsets (each irreducible closed subset has precisely one generic point) (Exercise 3.7.E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies points of Spec A with prime ideals and identifies irreducible closed subsets with closures of points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal primes correspond to irreducible components
rubrics_metrics.description: A prime ideal is minimal (a minimal prime) if it is minimal with respect to inclusion. The irreducible components of Spec A are in bijection with the minimal prime ideals of A; Spec A is irreducible iff A has only one minimal prime (Exercise/Definition 3.7.F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a consequence of Proposition 3.6.15 and Exercise 3.7.F, every Noetherian ring has finitely many minimal prime ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of structure sheaf OSpec A on distinguished opens
rubrics_metrics.description: Define OSpec A(D(f)) to be the localization of A at the multiplicative set of all functions that do not vanish outside of V(f) (i.e., those g in A such that V(g) ⊂ V(f)). This depends only on D(f), and not on f itself (Definition 4.1.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically this is Af under the usual identification; also OSpec A(∅) = {0} (Exercise 3.5.F). Restriction maps between distinguished opens are the natural localization maps; these define a presheaf on the distinguished base.

rubrics_metrics.name: OSpec A is a sheaf (base identity and gluability on distinguished base)
rubrics_metrics.description: The data described (sections on D(f) and restriction maps) give a sheaf on the distinguished base, and hence determine a sheaf on Spec A (Theorem 4.1.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof checks the base identity and base gluability axioms: base identity via quasicompactness and injectivity argument (exact sequence (4.1.3.1)), base gluability via a 'partition of unity' style argument reducing to finite subcovers, and handling infinite covers by finite subcover + base identity. Exercises 4.1.B and 4.1.C adapt the argument to arbitrary distinguished opens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of elements of A as functions on Spec A
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the construction of the structure sheaf, elements of A may be interpreted as global functions on Spec A: Γ(Spec A, OSpec A) = A (Remark 4.3.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justifies thinking of A as the ring of global sections on the affine scheme Spec A; more generally Γ(D(f), OSpec A) ≅ Af.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheaf associated to an A-module (quasi-coherent sheaf on distinguished base)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an A-module M, define M(D(f)) to be the localization of M at the multiplicative set of functions that do not vanish outside V(f). This construction describes a sheaf M on the distinguished base and makes M into an OSpec A-module (Exercise/Definition 4.1.D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the process you'll see exactness properties analogous to (4.1.3.1), and one can identify M with a specific submodule of the product of localizations when covering by finitely many distinguished opens (Remark 4.1.4). This underlies the notion of quasi-coherent sheaves developed later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stalks of the structure sheaf: OSpec A_{[p]} = A_p
rubrics_metrics.description: The stalk of OSpec A at the point [p] is the local ring A_p (Important easy exercise 4.3.F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus values/germs at a point are given by localization at the corresponding prime ideal; this identifies 'values at a point' with elements of the local ring and residue field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of affine scheme and scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: An affine scheme is a ringed space isomorphic to (Spec A, OSpec A) for some A. A scheme (X, OX) is a ringed space such that every point of X has an open neighborhood U with (U, OX|U) isomorphic to an affine scheme (Definition 4.3.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isomorphism of ringed spaces consists of a homeomorphism of underlying spaces together with an isomorphism of structure sheaves (via pullback).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovering ring from global sections of an affine scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: If (X, OX) is an affine scheme equal to Spec A, then Γ(X, OX) = A. More generally, given an affine scheme one may recover A by taking global sections (Remark 4.3.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 4.3.A asks to describe bijection between isomorphisms Spec A ≅ Spec A' and ring isomorphisms A' ≅ A; showing that the scheme structure determines the ring is a slightly subtle exercise (start by checking on points).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguished opens correspond to localizations Spec A_f
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the identification of D(f) in Spec A with Spec A_f, there is a natural isomorphism of ringed spaces (D(f), OSpec A|_{D(f)}) ≅ (Spec A_f, OSpec A_f) (Exercise 4.3.B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguished opens form a base for the Zariski topology and are themselves affine opens; use this to localize arguments and glue constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed subschemes: many scheme structures on a closed subset
rubrics_metrics.description: Closed subsets of a scheme can have many 'natural' scheme structures; for example, if I is an ideal, Spec A/I endows the closed subset V(I) with a scheme structure, but different ideals can have the same vanishing set (e.g., (x) and (x^2) in k[x]) (Remark 4.3.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding scheme-theoretic closed subsets requires distinguishing between the set-theoretic vanishing locus and the scheme structure (nilpotents, thickness, 'fuzz'), which will be developed further in §8.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization of nilpotents and nonreduced schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonradical ideals (nilpotents) should be pictured as points with infinitesimal 'fuzz' encoding derivative-like information: e.g., Spec C[x]/(x^2) is the origin with first-derivative fuzz; Spec C[x]/(x^3) remembers up to second derivative, etc. In two variables, ideals like (x^2,y) remember derivative information only in the x-direction (Section 4.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These visual heuristics (Figures 4.2–4.5) help interpret multiplicity and directionality of intersections (e.g., parabola y=x^2 intersecting x-axis gives Spec C[x,y]/(y,x^2), reflecting multiplicity two in x-direction). Later sections make 'location of fuzz' precise via associated points (Remark 13.7.2) and scheme-theoretic intersections (Exercise 8.1.J).
